subject: ela
intro: Reading fluency means reading smoothly, accurately, and with expression — the way people talk. A fluent reader does not read one word at a time like a robot. Instead, fluent readers group words into meaningful phrases, use punctuation as signals to pause or change their voice, and go back to fix mistakes when something does not make sense. Three key parts of fluency are: accuracy (reading the right words), rate (not too fast or too slow), and expression (reading with feeling and phrasing).

items.prompt:
A student reads this sentence two ways:
Way 1: 'The... cat... sat... on... the... mat.'
Way 2: 'The cat sat on the mat.'
Which way shows better reading fluency? Why?

steps: Way 1 reads each word separately — this is called word-by-word reading, which hurts comprehension.
Way 2 reads words in a smooth, natural flow — this is fluent reading.
Fluent readers group words together as they would say them in conversation.
Way 2 also helps the listener understand the meaning more easily.
solution.answer: Way 2 shows better fluency — words are read smoothly, not one at a time.

items.prompt: A student is reading and comes to a word she doesn't recognize. She skips it and keeps going. Is this a good strategy? What should she do instead?

steps: Skipping unknown words is not a good strategy — it can cause the reader to lose meaning.
A better strategy: try to sound out the word using phonics.
Another strategy: use the context of the sentence — what word would make sense here?
If still unsure, reread the sentence from the beginning.
Good readers self-correct and confirm their word recognition makes sense.
solution.answer: She should try to sound out the word and use context clues, then reread the sentence if needed. Skipping words hurts comprehension.

items.prompt: Why do good readers pay attention to punctuation (periods, commas, question marks) when reading aloud?

steps: Punctuation tells readers how to use their voice.
A period means pause and drop your voice — the idea is complete.
A comma means a brief pause within a sentence.
A question mark means raise your voice at the end — you are asking something.
An exclamation point means read with energy and feeling.
Reading punctuation correctly helps listeners understand the meaning.
solution.answer: Punctuation signals pauses and voice changes that help the reader communicate meaning clearly.

items.prompt: A student reads a sentence and then says, 'That didn't sound right.' She goes back and rereads. What reading skill is she using?

steps: The student is using self-monitoring — she checks whether her reading makes sense.
When something sounds wrong, a good reader stops and goes back.
This is called self-correction or rereading for self-correction.
It is a sign of a skilled, thoughtful reader who cares about meaning.
solution.answer: She is using self-monitoring and self-correction — key fluency skills.

items.prompt: What does it mean to read with 'expression'? Give an example.

steps: Reading with expression means using your voice to show meaning and feeling.
Example: 'WATCH OUT!' should be read loudly and urgently.
'He crept quietly through the dark house.' should be read in a soft, slow voice.
Expression makes reading interesting and helps show the characters' feelings.
Reading everything in the same flat voice (monotone) is a sign of poor fluency.
solution.answer: Expression means using voice, speed, and emphasis to match the meaning and feeling of the text.

items.prompt:
A student reads: 'She... likes... to... play... in... the... park.' Is this fluent reading?
A) Yes
B) No — it is too slow and choppy
items.hint: Think about how a fluent reader groups words together.

steps: Reading each word one at a time with pauses between every word is choppy and non-fluent.
A fluent reader would read: 'She likes to play / in the park.' — grouping words into phrases.
solution.answer: B) No. This is choppy, word-by-word reading. A fluent reader would group words into phrases.

items.prompt:
A student reads 'The big dog' as 'The bag dog.' She does not notice the mistake. What should she do?
A) Keep reading — it is close enough.
B) Go back and reread to self-correct.

steps: 'The bag dog' does not make sense.
A fluent reader self-monitors — she checks whether her reading makes sense.
She should go back, reread, and correct 'bag' to 'big'.
solution.answer: B) She should go back and reread to self-correct the error.

items.prompt:
Which reading rate is best for a Grade 1 reader?
A) Reading as fast as possible to get through the book
B) Reading at a steady pace that is easy to understand
C) Reading as slowly as possible to be careful
items.hint: Think about what helps the listener understand the story.

steps: Reading too fast makes it hard for a listener (or the reader) to understand.
Reading too slowly sounds choppy and loses the meaning.
A steady, comfortable rate supports comprehension for both the reader and the listener.
solution.answer: B) A steady, comfortable pace that supports understanding.

items.prompt:
A reader sees this sentence: 'Did you see the rainbow?' How should the reader's voice change at the end?
A) Drop the voice at the end
B) Raise the voice at the end
C) Stay flat the whole time
items.hint: Look at the punctuation mark at the end.

steps: The sentence ends with a question mark (?).
Questions usually have the voice rising at the end.
A rising voice signals to the listener that a question is being asked.
solution.answer: B) Raise the voice at the end.

items.prompt:
Why is it helpful for a reader to reread a sentence they did not understand the first time?
A) To read faster next time
B) To check understanding and correct any mistakes
C) Because it is fun
items.hint: Think about the purpose of rereading.

steps: Rereading helps the reader catch errors and think more carefully about the meaning.
This is a self-monitoring strategy — good readers check that what they read makes sense.
Rereading is not about reading faster; it is about reading accurately and for meaning.
solution.answer: B) To check understanding and correct any mistakes.
